analysis.one_liner: Repeals the entire Affordable Care Act and restores the health care law in place before it.
analysis.headline: A full repeal of the Affordable Care Act drew 105 cosponsors, but the bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act retroactively, as if it had never passed, and put back the health care laws that existed before it [S2] [S3]. That means undoing the law's coverage expansion, its subsidies to help people buy insurance, its new rules on insurers, and its tax and fee provisions. The bill was introduced days after the ACA became law, referred to eight committees, and never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's direct beneficiaries are concentrated: high-income households, who would avoid the ACA's additional Medicare payroll tax on wages above the threshold; brand-name drug makers and medical device makers, whose new annual fees and excise taxes would disappear; and insurers, who would shed the law's consumer rules and its annual fee. Some ordinary people who opposed the mandate to buy insurance would also welcome repeal, but they would give up the law's coverage subsidies and protections to get it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, drug makers, device makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA retroactively, effective as of its enactment, and restores every provision of law the ACA amended or repealed [S2] [S3].
The bill was introduced with 105 cosponsors — 104 of the 178 House Republicans and 1 of the 253 House Democrats — showing broad Republican support for full repeal [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the entire cost. Repealing the ACA and restoring pre-ACA law would end the subsidies that help moderate-income people buy coverage, the expansion of Medicaid, the rule allowing young adults to stay on a parent's insurance plan, and the coming protections that bar insurers from denying or dropping coverage based on health status — rules that existed because pre-ACA law allowed insurers to do all of those things.
analysis.who_pays_short: People who gained ACA coverage and protections

drawbacks.text: The core of the bill is eliminating coverage, not reforming it: by restoring the law as it stood before the ACA, it would re-expose people to insurance practices the ACA prohibited, such as lifetime benefit limits and medical underwriting [S3].

A good-faith objection supporters would acknowledge: full repeal offered no replacement, so even voters unhappy with the ACA's mandate would lose its benefits — subsidies, dependent coverage to age 26, and eventual pre-existing-condition protections — with nothing in their place [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is almost purely one-sided. Its tangible gains go to a narrow set of interests — high earners facing a new Medicare payroll tax and industries facing new fees — while its costs fall on the millions of people the ACA was written to cover. Even supporters who honestly opposed the individual mandate had to admit that repeal with no replacement took away far more than it returned to most households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in eight committees without a hearing, and its sponsor's attempt to force it out of committee with a discharge petition never produced a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 25, 2010, days after the ACA was enacted, and referred to eight House committees at once, with no lead committee ever acting on it [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to subcommittees on Health and on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions in April 2010 and never advanced [S5].

On June 16, 2010, sponsor Rep. Steve King filed a motion to discharge the committees — a device that requires a majority of House members to sign a petition to force a bill out of committee and onto the floor — but the bill never received a vote [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the ACA's provisions stayed in place: people who had just gained coverage through the new law — young adults on their parents' plans, people buying subsidized insurance, and those who would later be protected from pre-existing-condition denials — kept those gains, while high earners and the drug, device, and insurance industries remained subject to the ACA's taxes and fees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who kept ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill and later filed a discharge petition attempting to pull it out of committee for a floor vote without committee approval.

for.name: 104 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to repeal the ACA in its entirety.

for.name: 1 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill, the only Democratic member to do so.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Held the House majority and controlled the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote, leaving it stranded in committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chaired the eight committees of referral, including Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican: 104 of 178 House Republicans signed on, against a single Democrat among 253, in a chamber the Democrats controlled 253 to 178.

industries.note: Repeal would have erased the ACA's annual fee on branded prescription drugs, which helped finance the law's coverage expansion. The industry's savings would have come directly out of the coverage pool ordinary people draw on.
Repeal would have ended the ACA's excise tax on medical devices. The industry's gain was the public's loss of the revenue that funded subsidies and protections.
Repeal would have removed the ACA's additional Medicare payroll tax on high wages, cutting taxes for the highest earners while eliminating the programs those taxes supported.

Repeal would have freed insurers from the ACA's annual fee and its consumer rules, but also from the individual mandate and subsidies that delivered them millions of new customers. On balance, the industry's interest lay in weakening the law's requirements rather than keeping its coverage protections.
